title: Rotate a Grid 90 Degrees

statement.md: A correlation heat-map export needs to be rotated 90° clockwise for a report layout. Rotate the $n \times n$ grid: the top row becomes the right column, the left column becomes the top row.

inputFormat: First line: $n$ ($1 \le n \le 1000$). Then $n$ rows of $n$ tokens.
outputFormat: The rotated grid, $n$ rows of $n$ tokens.

examples.explanation: First row (1 2 3) becomes the last column; read column 1 bottom-up (7 4 1) to get the new first row.

hints: Derive the index map: new[i][j] = old[n-1-j][i].
Verify with the 2x2 case by hand before coding the general n.

editorial.md: The whole problem is one index relation: after a clockwise rotation, the element at old position $(r, c)$ lands at new $(c, n-1-r)$ — equivalently `new[i][j] = old[n-1-j][i]`. Derive it (don't memorise) from where the corners go: top-left (0,0) must become top-right (0, n-1).

The in-place variant (four-way cycle swaps, layer by layer) matters in C++ when $n$ is large and you cannot afford a second grid — a memory-habits question more than an algorithms one. In interviews, expect the follow-up: rotate counter-clockwise (reverse the relation), or rotate $k$ times (compose, don't loop).

solutions.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
g = [data[1+i*n:1+(i+1)*n] for i in range(n)]
res = [[g[n-1-j][i] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
print("\n".join(" ".join(row) for row in res))

tests.input:
3
x y z
p q r
m n o
tests.expected:
